boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Pasewalk entry (capitulation, 29 October 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: General Milhaud's cavalry brigade, pursuing for Murat, and the Prussian column at Pasewalk under Colonel Hagen, his infantry brigade with Colonel Poser's cavalry, from its arrival at Pasewalk on the 28th to the capitulation on the morning of the 29th. The detachments that got away before the capitulation and the prisoners' march to Prenzlow are context. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side B (Prussian) as 4,200 Prussians (among them 185 officers) with 2,100 horses, 8 guns and 1 ammunition wagon under Brigadier Colonel v. Hagen, who capitulated before Milhaud's French cavalry brigade (side A, French) of 700 riders. By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner's table totals 185 officers, 4043 men, 2087 horses, 8 guns and 1 powder wagon, and his officers and men together 4228 (our arithmetic); Milhaud gives his own brigade as 600 horse (claims side-b-strength, side-b-strength-french, side-a-strength). English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 29/10. capitulation of Pasewalk'; 'before the French cavalry brigade Milhaud (700 riders) 4,200 Prussians (among them 185 officers) capitulate with 2,100 horses, 8 guns, 1 ammunition wagon under Brigadier Colonel v. Hagen, after which the officers were released on their word of honour and the men led off into captivity'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) in Höpfner: Colonel Hagen's infantry brigade, ordered on the night to the 28th to a rendezvous on the road from Fürstenwerder to Pasewalk, found no cavalry there; only after sending out officers did it find, at some distance, 2 squadrons of Katte dragoons and the rest of the Bailliodz cuirassiers under Lieutenant Colonel Stülpnagel, which were to march with it to Pasewalk; the cavalry brigade Podewils, the Leib-Karabiniers and the Heising, Holtzendorf, Bünting and Henckel cuirassiers, followed to Pasewalk under Colonel Poser. Höpfner's table of what they handed to the enemy, whom they had not even seen: 75 officers and 1957 men of the infantry brigade Hagen; 110 officers, 2086 men and 2087 horses of the cavalry; in all 185 officers, 4043 men, 2087 horses, 8 guns and 1 powder wagon. Elsewhere he speaks of Hagen's 2000 men. Stülpnagel with the Bailliodz cuirassiers and the 2 Katte squadrons, Colonel Schubärt, Rittmeister Trotha's detachment and the quartermaster Langheinrich with the baggage of the Feldjäger regiment got away.
claims.rationale: Side B's history: the table and the escapes from the page images of pp. 214-216, the composition from the page image of p. 209 and the OCR of p. 210. No fighting took place, so the troops handed over are the force present at the capitulation, the escapes before it being given separately; the force was brought from the retreat, so the claim is tagged inherited. Höpfner's 2000 is a round figure for Hagen's infantry beside the table's 75 officers and 1957 men. The OCR reads one regiment 'Hei- fing', taken here as Heising, the regiment of Major Thielan 'von Heiſing' on p. 211. English renderings (ours): 'the infantry brigade Hagen received in the night to the 28th in its quarters at Fürstenwerder from General Count Schwerin the order to hold itself ready, as the enemy was near, to set out at the first sign, and soon afterwards came a note with the instruction to stand ready at 5 o'clock in the morning at Rittgarten, north of Schapow and on the road from Fürstenwerder to Pasewalk'; 'the brigade arrived at the rendezvous at the appointed time, but found no cavalry there, and only after several officers had been sent out, at some distance, 2 squadrons of Katte dragoons and the rest of the Bailliodz cuirassier regiment under Lieutenant Colonel Stülpnagel, which had the order to march with the brigade Hagen to Pasewalk'; 'the cavalry brigade Podewils — Leib-Karabiniers, Hei-fing, Holtzendorf, Bünting and Henckel cuirassiers — had likewise come to the rendezvous, waited there long for the brigadier, Colonel Podewils, and had at last followed to Pasewalk under Colonel Poser, of the Henckel cuirassier regiment' (OCR); 'they gave into the hands of the enemy, whom they had not even seen: 75 officers | 1957 men | of the infantry brigade Hagen; 110 ditto | 2086 ditto | 2087 horses of the cavalry; together: 185 officers | 4043 men | 2087 horses, 8 guns and 1 powder wagon'; 'if Colonel Hagen believed he could not ask the infantry to march early, he found in Pasewalk over 100 townsmen-farmers and in the numerous villages nearby so many teams and so much good will that he could well have carried his 2000 men safely away on wagons after a halt of several hours'; 'that one could escape is proved by the escape of Colonel Schubärt of the Quitzow cuirassiers, the detachment of Rittmeister Trotha of the Leib cuirassier regiment, the regimental quartermaster Langheinrich with the baggage of the Feldjäger regiment, and Lieutenant Colonel Stülpnagel with Bailliodz cuirassiers and 2 squadrons of Katte dragoons'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), side A's (French) figures: Milhaud wrote to Belliard on 30 October that with a brigade of 600 horse he had faced 2,000 Prussian cavalry and 3,000 infantry, that 2,000 cavalry had had to be made to dismount before a handful of men, and that he was marching off with 36 flags and 5,000 prisoners; nearly 1,000 horses had had to be left in the closed meadow or in the town, and at least 2 horses were led per man. Murat wrote on 30 October that Milhaud had made a corps of 6,000 men lay down its arms at Pasewalk, and the 24th Bulletin, a column of 6,000.
claims.rationale: Side A's figures, read from the page images; not reconciled with Höpfner's table or Bodart's figures (claims side-b-strength, bodart-strength). Milhaud's 2,000 and 3,000 are his estimate of the force he faced and his 5,000 the prisoners he was escorting; the 6,000 of Murat and the Bulletin are round statements. Murat's letter to Bernadotte of 29 October, printed in a footnote on p. 524, also gives figures for Pasewalk, seen only in the OCR and not restated. The force was brought from the retreat, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): Milhaud, 'General Milhaud to General Belliard. Prenzlow, 30 October 1806'; 'in spite of the difficult position in which I found myself, with a brigade of 600 horse against 2,000 Prussian cavalry and 3,000 infantry, I granted them only a severe capitulation'; 'I assure you that many precautions had to be taken to make 2,000 cavalry dismount before a handful of men; I ordered all the prisoners to be filed off to Prenzlow'; 'we were obliged to leave nearly 1,000 horses in the closed meadow or in the town; we set out having at least 2 horses led per man; I had drawn in the 2 elite companies to carry the 36 flags or standards, which were laid down with the arms in the middle of our ranks'; 'we leave Prenzlow today to make for the Emperor's headquarters with the 36 flags and the 5,000 prisoners; my aide de camp and M. Paskowski, attached to your staff, gave me His Imperial Highness's verbal order to escort our prisoners myself, with my 2 regiments'; Murat, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Löcknitz, 30 October 1806, 2 o'clock in the morning'; 'while General Milhaud was making a corps of 6,000 men lay down its arms at Pasewalk, General'; the Bulletin, '24th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 31 October 1806'; 'Stettin is in our power. While the left of the Grand Duke of Berg, commanded by General Milhaud, was making a column of 6,000 men lay down its arms at Pasewalk, the right, commanded by General Lasalle, was summoning the town of Stettin and imposing on it the capitulation attached'.

claims.value: Side A (French): Murat wrote on 28 October that General Milhaud was following the enemy with the 13th chasseurs and the 9th dragoons, and that Milhaud was moving on Pasewalk. Milhaud describes his force as a brigade of 600 horse, a handful of men, and 'my 2 regiments', which Foucart's note identifies as the 13th chasseurs and the 9th dragoons of Beaumont's division. Bodart gives Milhaud's brigade 700 riders. Höpfner says the Prussians handed themselves over to an enemy they had not even seen; the chasseur officer who had accompanied Count Matuschka claimed to have no instructions and asked that an officer be sent to General Milhaud, who stood nearby, and a parlementaire from Lasalle's cavalry also came, so that 3 were present. No passage read gives a return of Milhaud's regiments.
claims.rationale: Murat's and Milhaud's letters, Foucart's note and Höpfner's account read from the page images. Milhaud's 600 is his own figure for his brigade; Bodart's 700 is not reconciled with it. English renderings (ours): Murat, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Prenzlow, 28 October 1806'; 'at 6 o'clock in the morning I was on the march with all the cavalry to support General Lasalle. General Milhaud was following the enemy with the 13th chasseurs and the 9th dragoons'; 'General Lasalle is marching on Löcknitz, where he will sleep this evening, to cut off General Blücher's retreat; General Milhaud is moving on Pasewalk; tomorrow I shall be on Stettin'; Milhaud, as in claim side-b-strength-french for the heading, his brigade, the handful of men and his 2 regiments; Foucart's note, '13th chasseurs and 9th dragoons, of Beaumont's division'; Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Höpfner, as in claim side-b-strength for the enemy not seen; 'it was the chasseur officer who had accompanied Count Matuschka, but who claimed to have no instructions and therefore had to ask that an officer be sent to General Milhaud, who stood nearby'; 'finally Lieutenant Kölichen also came with a parlementaire from General Lasalle's cavalry, whom he claimed to have met a mile from Löcknitz, so probably at Berkholz, so that 3 parlementaires were now present'.

claims.rationale: Bodart's printed commanders. claims.value: Side A's command: Murat reported Milhaud following the enemy and moving on Pasewalk. By Milhaud's account he granted only a severe capitulation, the soldiers going as prisoners to France and the officers owing their freedom on parole only to the Grand Duke's generosity; he took many precautions to make 2,000 cavalry dismount before a handful of men, and had the prisoners filed off to Prenzlow. In Höpfner, the chasseur officer who had accompanied Count Matuschka claimed to have no instructions and asked that an officer be sent to General Milhaud, standing nearby; Lieutenant Hohendorf returned with Lieutenant Colonel Guillaume, who had full powers from the Grand Duke of Berg, a capitulation was drafted, and it was sent to the Grand Duke at Löcknitz for ratification. The Grand Duke, to whom the Prussian lieutenants Madalinski and Bassewitz had been brought, sent Madalinski back with a negotiator and kept Bassewitz.
claims.rationale: Murat's and Milhaud's letters and Höpfner's account read from the page images, with Höpfner's account of the officers sent out from the OCR. The terms Milhaud describes were his own choice by his letter; the ratification by the Grand Duke is Höpfner's. English renderings (ours): Murat, as in claim side-a-strength for 28 October; Milhaud, as in claim side-b-strength-french for the heading, the severe capitulation and the dismounting; 'you will have observed that all the soldiers are prisoners in France and that the officers owe their liberty, on their word of honour, only to the generosity of His Imperial Highness the Grand Duke of Berg'; Höpfner, 'Lieutenant Count Matuschka had met the enemy in a village and had carried out Colonel Poser's errand, and a French chasseur officer had at once been sent to Pasewalk' (OCR); as in claim side-a-strength for the chasseur officer; 'Lieutenant Hohendorf soon came back with Lieutenant Colonel Guillaume, who had been given full powers by the Grand Duke of Berg and was accompanied by Lieutenant Madalinski. A capitulation was now drafted, which was sent to the Grand Duke at Löcknitz for ratification'; 'Lieutenants Madalinski and Count Bassewitz had met the enemy on the road to Löcknitz' (OCR); 'and been taken to the Grand Duke of Berg, who sent Lieutenant Madalinski back with a negotiator but kept Count Bassewitz with him'.

claims.value: Höpfner: Colonel Hagen, as the eldest of the column, called all the staff officers of the infantry and cavalry to a conference. Before it, Colonel Poser told the cavalry's staff officers that Prince Hohenlohe had capitulated and the pass at Löcknitz was occupied, so that they would have to cut their way through; Major Thielan of the Heising regiment spoke first of the difficulties a break-through faced with men and horses exhausted and told Lieutenant Prittwitz, who declared a capitulation dishonourable, to be quiet; Colonel Winning of the Leib-Karabiniers consulted not only his officers but also called into counsel the sergeant-major of each squadron with NCOs and men, and that meeting resolved that they could not cut through but must capitulate. Several staff officers urged Poser to set out for Stettin as soon as possible. At the conference Hagen said he lacked the knowledge to judge whether the cavalry could march on; the Landrat Podewils proposed a safe route by Jägerbrück and Stolzenburg, and the colonel, by the context Hagen, paid no heed. Poser posted no field guards and ordered no patrols, only a chain of posts round the bivouac whose officers were to meet the enemy with a trumpeter and tell him negotiations were under way, and sent officer after officer to find the enemy, Count Matuschka with orders to tell him of their sad situation and bring back an officer of higher rank to capitulate, but by no means to reconnoitre. When Prince Gustav of Mecklenburg-Schwerin reported the cavalry ever more enclosed and saw no way out but capitulation, Hagen, physically and morally exhausted and deeply bowed by Prenzlau, was confirmed in a resolve to capitulate that Höpfner says Poser seems to have prompted. Hagen and Poser signed a written mandate to capitulate for the two brigades with free withdrawal or, failing that, to surrender them into captivity. Höpfner finds no justification of any kind for the capitulation: the commanders thought of nothing but capitulation and sent officers in all directions to seek out the enemy and offer themselves.
claims.rationale: Side B's history: the mandate, the parlementaire and Höpfner's judgment from the page images of pp. 214-215, the conferences and the officers sent out from the OCR of pp. 210-213. Höpfner does not name his sources for Pasewalk. NCO and ... men' (OCR); 'and the decision of this meeting was that they could not cut their way through but must capitulate' (OCR); 'several staff officers urgently pressed Colonel Poser to set out for Stettin as soon as possible' (OCR); 'after all the staff officers had gathered in the evening at Colonel Hagen's in Pasewalk, he declared to the officers of the cavalry that he had not enough knowledge of their situation to be able to judge whether they were able to march on or not. The cavalry officers declared that men and horses were very exhausted, but that an early march was nevertheless advisable' (OCR); 'he reported that by the statement of a man arrived from Löcknitz the road to Stettin was free, but that he proposed, for safety's sake, to march through the great Fichthaide by Jägerbrück and Stolzenburg, where the enemy could do them no harm. Because of the difficulty of the crossing he advised against a march to the island of Usedom' (OCR); 'the colonel paid no heed to this statement' (OCR); 'Colonel Poser arranged that for the night no field guards were posted and no patrolling ordered, but only a chain of posts drawn round the bivouac of the cavalry, whose commanding officers received the instruction, if the enemy approached, to enter into no hostilities but to go to meet him with a trumpeter and inform him that negotiations were already under way' (OCR); 'at midnight Colonel Poser further sent off Lieutenant Count Königsdorf of the Henckel cuirassiers with a trumpeter and ... men' (OCR); 'when this officer came back without having perceived anything of the enemy, Colonel Poser sent Lieutenant Count Matuschka of the same regiment with the same escort, but with the errand to ride straight on until he came upon the enemy, to inform him of their sad situation, and to bring back an officer of higher rank to capitulate, but by no means to make a reconnaissance' (OCR); 'when Count Matuschka stayed away too long for Colonel Poser, Lieutenants Madalinski of the Bünting and' (OCR); 'Count Bassewitz of the Henckel cuirassiers, and towards morning Lieutenant Schkopp, were sent off with the same errands' (OCR); 'he rode to Pasewalk to Colonel Hagen and reported to him: the cavalry was being more and more enclosed by the enemy' (OCR); 'Colonel Hagen asked the Prince what was to be done, as the cavalry's horses were too exhausted to accept a fight' (OCR); 'the Prince found a way out only in capitulation' (OCR); 'this view of the Prince strengthened in Colonel Hagen, who was physically and morally quite exhausted by the unspeakable hardships but deeply bowed by the capitulation of Prenzlau, the resolve already taken after the ... conference to capitulate as well, though Colonel Poser seems to have prompted the very idea' (OCR); 'Lieutenant Hohendorf was sent off, accompanied by an enemy chasseur, with the written mandate signed by Colonels Hagen and Poser: to capitulate for the two brigades and stipulate free withdrawal, or if this were not granted, to deliver them into captivity'; 'if the capitulation at Prenzlau, where they knew a strong cavalry to be facing them and, by Colonel Massenbach's statements, could assume a strong enemy in their rear, where the troops had to cover a road of almost 4 miles across the plain in the face of the enemy in complete exhaustion and almost without ammunition, still had a trace of justification, the capitulation of Pasewalk had none of any kind'; 'they were informed early of the events at Prenzlau, and so knew of the enemy's approach; nevertheless no patrols are sent out to learn the enemy's position; no attempt is made, by spending their last strength, to forestall the enemy at Löcknitz; nor, if they believed they could not risk this attempt, do they take the trouble to inquire whether other roads than that by Löcknitz to Stettin were free; they pay no heed to the statement of the Landrat Podewils, who shows such a road; claims.value: Bodart records the capitulation of Pasewalk on 29 October before Milhaud's brigade: the officers were released on their word of honour and the men led off into captivity. Höpfner: the terms were that the troops should lay down their arms, the officers be released on their word of honour and the privates be led off as prisoners of war; the draft was sent to the Grand Duke of Berg at Löcknitz for ratification. Milhaud wrote that he granted only a severe capitulation, all the soldiers prisoners in France and the officers free on parole only by the Grand Duke's generosity, and that the 36 flags or standards were laid down with the arms in the middle of his ranks. Murat and the 24th Bulletin report the corps laying down its arms to Milhaud.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome with Höpfner's account and the French letters, read from the page images; no source read gives a different result. Neither source read prints the capitulation's text. Höpfner's heading dates it 29 October, and his narrative places it on the morning after the conferences of the evening of the 28th, before the troops set out. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Höpfner, 'the capitulation at Pasewalk, 29 October'; 'the conditions of the capitulation were that the troops should lay down their arms, the officers be released on their word of honour and the privates be led off into captivity as prisoners of war'; as in claim side-a-command for the draft sent for ratification; 'before the troops had yet set out from Pasewalk, the arrival of an enemy parlementaire was reported to Colonel Hagen from the gate'; Milhaud, as in claims side-b-strength-french for the heading, the severe capitulation and the flags and side-a-command for the terms; Murat and the Bulletin, as in claim side-b-strength-french.

claims.value: Höpfner: on the march the brigade heard the cannonade at Prenzlau. At Pasewalk all the news, especially the statement of Colonel Schubärt of the Quitzow cuirassiers, showed the enemy very near and the danger of being enclosed; Lieutenant Meyer brought news of the capitulation at Prenzlau, confirmed by Lieutenant Vogel, General Tauentzien's adjutant; Colonel Poser told the cavalry's staff officers that the pass at Löcknitz was occupied; Lieutenant Colonel Stülpnagel reported that he had news of an unlucky action at Prenzlau and would set out at once for Löcknitz. The Landrat Podewils, come from Stettin that evening, reported that by a man arrived from Löcknitz the road to Stettin was free. Poser's officers were sent to find the enemy but not to reconnoitre; the first came back having perceived nothing; in the night Prince Gustav of Mecklenburg-Schwerin believed he saw movements by moonlight on the Prenzlau and Stettin roads. Höpfner says the Prussians had not even seen the enemy to whom they surrendered, sent out no patrols, made no inquiry whether other roads than that by Löcknitz were free, and ignored the Landrat.
claims.rationale: From the history of side B: the judgment and the heading of the table from the page images of pp. 214-215, the rest from the OCR of pp. 210-213. open_questions: Deferred: Murat's letter to Bernadotte of 29 October, printed in a footnote that begins on Foucart t. II, p. 523, outside the registered section, whose heading and text were read only in the OCR, with its figures for Pasewalk; the Emperor's letter to Soult of 31 October (pp. 556-557); the capitulation's text, which neither source read prints; a French return of the prisoners, horses and flags; the records of the Prussian judicial inquiries held after the war, on which by the preface of his first volume Höpfner's work chiefly rests. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated: the hours of the march, the conferences and the intended departures (Höpfner, pp. 210-212), Lieutenant Meyer's horses (p. 210), the men consulted by Colonel Winning and sent with Count Königsdorf (pp. 211-212), the figures in Murat's footnote letter (Foucart, p. 524) and in the Emperor's letter to Soult (p. 557).

Most consequential gap: side A's strength. Milhaud's own figure is a brigade of 600 horse in 2 regiments, Bodart's is 700, and no return of the 13th chasseurs and 9th dragoons was read; whether any other French troops were near enough to count (Lasalle's parlementaire came from the Löcknitz road) is not shown, and Höpfner says the Prussians never saw the enemy. A return of Milhaud's brigade could settle it.

Disputes kept as separate claims: side B's strength (Höpfner's 185 officers and 4043 men with 2087 horses, 8 guns and 1 powder wagon, and Hagen's 2000 infantry; Bodart's 4,200 with 185 officers, 2,100 horses, 8 guns and 1 ammunition wagon; Milhaud's 2,000 cavalry and 3,000 infantry and 5,000 prisoners; the 6,000 of Murat and the Bulletin); side A (Milhaud's 600 horse, Bodart's 700); the flags (36, Milhaud; none counted by Höpfner or Bodart); who received the capitulation (Milhaud, by Bodart and the French letters; a negotiator with powers from the Grand Duke, by Höpfner, the draft going to the Grand Duke at Löcknitz for ratification).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked, though his 185 officers, 8 guns and 1 wagon are Höpfner's figures); Foucart, t. II (the French side's documents: Murat's letters of 28 and 30 October, Milhaud's letter to Belliard with Foucart's note, the 24th Bulletin); Höpfner, Bd. 2, 2nd edition (the Prussian side's history; by the preface of his first volume the work rests chiefly on the records of the judicial inquiries held after the war, but the Pasewalk passage names no source).
